title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
formal: Given a bipartite graph $G=(L\cup R,E)$ with $|L|=|R|=n$, a red/blue coloring of its edges, and $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, decide whether $G$ has a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The historical question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the ordinary bit encoding of $(G,k)$. An April 2026 preprint claims such an algorithm. This entry records that claimed resolution and its verification limits; it is no longer labeled as a confirmed open problem.
why: I retain and expand this entry because exact cardinality constraints can remain difficult even when unconstrained optimization is easy. It is also a useful status correction: a research catalogue should preserve the problem and the claimed advance, while distinguishing an attributed preprint theorem from a proof that has been independently checked.

title: Can reachability diameter be approximated within a constant in near-linear time?
formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least 2/3 in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving D(G)=0 on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.

title: Erdős girth conjecture: is the classical spanner size bound tight?
formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge 2$, do there exist a constant $c_k>0$ and arbitrarily large simple undirected graphs $G$ with $n$ vertices, at least $c_k n^{1+1/k}$ edges, and no cycle of length at most $2k$? Equivalently, can the $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ extremal upper bound for girth greater than $2k$ be attained up to a constant factor for every $k$? The first unsettled value is $k=4$: girth at least nine and $\Omega(n^{5/4})$ edges.
why: This is a structural problem with a short, rigorous reduction to an algorithmic limit. I include it because many claims that a distance-preserving graph representation is optimal depend on precisely this unproved construction. A proof would establish those lower bounds; a counterexample would force a re-examination of the expected stretch–space tradeoff.

title: Can exact weighted all-pairs shortest paths be computed in truly subcubic time?
formal: Is there a constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every n-vertex directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, outputs all exact shortest-path distances in $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ worst-case time with probability at least 2/3? Use a comparison-addition real RAM: adding, subtracting, and comparing stored real values costs O(1), and standard arithmetic and bit operations on O(log n)-bit index words cost O(1). Unreachable distances must be reported as infinity. Arbitrary real-number encodings or unit-cost floor operations are unavailable.
why: I include this because exact distances are a basic graph primitive, and this particular exponent question organizes many conditional lower bounds. A resolution would identify either a common algorithmic improvement across equivalent problems or a precise limitation of what those reductions can accomplish.

title: Is Exact Matching on general graphs in deterministic polynomial time?
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\le k\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.
why: I include this because it is a concrete combinatorial derandomization target with a short, checkable definition. It asks whether randomness is necessary for an exact constraint on top of an otherwise tractable optimization problem, connecting matching algorithms to algebraic identity testing.
